CausalChain: Dysregulated cell cycle in NSCLC -> Altered exosome biogenesis and cargo selection -> Reduced exosomal miR-200 levels -> Sustained EMT and enhanced cancer stem cell features -> Increased chemoresistance; Therefore, restoring proper cell cycle checkpoint function -> Promotes exosomal enrichment of miR-200 -> Induces MET and diminishes stemness -> Enhanced chemosensitivity.
Hypothesis: Modulating cell cycle checkpoints in NSCLC can reinstate exosomal miR‐200 enrichment, thereby reversing EMT and cancer stem cell properties to overcome chemoresistance, offering a novel therapeutic strategy.
Abstract: This hypothesis emerges from a comprehensive review of the complex interplay between microRNAs, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), cancer stem cell traits, and drug resistance across several tumor types. Although many studies have delineated how miRNAs such as the miR‐200 family, miR‐128‐3p, and others modulate EMT and chemoresistance, emerging evidence suggests that the cell cycle status may also govern the repertoire of miRNAs packaged into exosomes. In non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), altered cell cycle dynamics may influence the exosomal loading of key regulators like the miR‐200 family. Our hypothesis proposes that modulating cell cycle checkpoints to restore optimal miR‐200 levels in exosomes can induce a mesenchymal–to–epithelial transition (MET), reduce cancer stemness, and thereby overcome drug resistance.
